summary: Initial public knowledge catalog for Frontend Setup. Contains bounded guidance only; it does not contain executable recipes or change local scaffold templates.

guidance: Keep Server Components as the default and add client boundaries only where interaction requires them.
Create route groups only when they represent meaningful layout or navigation boundaries.
Keep route entry files focused; place reusable composition and infrastructure outside app routes.
Keep the app entry and routing layer thin; put shared UI and domain-specific behavior in clearly owned modules.
Use local component state first and add shared state or server-cache dependencies only when the use case needs them.
Keep API contracts and request handling separate from presentational components.
Prefer .astro components and static rendering for content that does not require client-side interactivity.
Add hydrated islands only for the interactive parts that need them; do not introduce React solely for animation.
Keep route files aligned with Astro conventions and share layouts through src/layouts.
Use React Native components and TypeScript design tokens; do not carry browser CSS or DOM manipulation into native code.
Prefer React Native Reanimated for complex motion and gestures, while using native capabilities for simpler transitions.
Respect Expo SDK compatibility when installing native dependencies; use Expo-aware installation where appropriate.
Keep route definitions and data-loading behavior aligned with the selected React Router mode.
Use nested layouts for genuine shared UI boundaries and keep route-level components focused.
Do not add a separate global server-state cache when the router's data APIs already cover the use case.
Use native ES modules and progressive enhancement instead of introducing a framework for simple pages.
Keep shared tokens in CSS and use BEM-style kebab-case classes for component naming.
Use data attributes for declarative behavior targets, with explicit cleanup for listeners and observers.
Optimize for one clear user journey and keep the page structure shallow.
Use motion to clarify hierarchy or guide attention; avoid animation that delays the primary action.
Share navigation, footer, and page shells without turning every section into a global abstraction.
Include metadata, semantic headings, accessible links, and responsive layouts from the start.
Keep content shape and content rendering separate so the source can change without rewriting page composition.
Account for metadata, article semantics, image dimensions, and missing-content states.
Make loading, empty, error, permission, and success states explicit for data-driven views.
Use server-state caching and global client state only where their distinct responsibilities are needed.
Let domain boundaries emerge from actual product responsibilities rather than scaffolding every possible feature folder.
Keep validation, API contracts, and error behavior explicit at application boundaries.
Define token semantics, component variants, accessibility expectations, and naming rules as a documented contract.
Keep primitive tokens distinct from semantic tokens and component-specific tokens.
Select the animation architecture based on interaction complexity; use native or CSS capabilities where they are sufficient.
Respect reduced-motion preferences and clean up timelines, observers, and event listeners.
